review_notes: The file is only 36 lines: one def and one lemma. I read the whole file. I grepped Mathlib for uses of HasFiniteMulSupport and HasFiniteSupport and for any existing unfolding or iff lemma, and found none. I did not find any competing simp rules or cycles. The one finding is a missing unfolding lemma, and I'm moderately confident in it. Without running Lean I can't confirm how simp behaves on these goals. findings.excerpt: def HasFiniteMulSupport (f : α → M) : Prop := f.mulSupport.Finite
findings.problem: The predicate is a plain, non-reducible def and has no unfolding lemma such as an `Iff.rfl` statement `HasFiniteMulSupport f ↔ f.mulSupport.Finite`. There is no `@[simp]` unfolding rule either. So Mathlib users who want to move to the `Set.Finite` API on `mulSupport` or `support` have to unfold the definition by hand. The repeated pattern is `simp [HasFiniteMulSupport]`, `rw [HasFiniteMulSupport, mulSupport]`, and `simp only [Function.HasFiniteMulSupport, Function.mulSupport, ne_eq]`. This includes the file's own lemma `hasFiniteMulSupport_one`, which uses `simp [HasFiniteMulSupport]`. Unfolding by definition name is brittle. It also exposes the raw `{x | f x ≠ 1}` set instead of the canonical `mulSupport` form, which is why some call sites also have to unfold `mulSupport` and then clean up with `ne_eq`.
findings.proposed_change: Add right after the def a named unfolding lemma, e.g. `@[to_additive] lemma hasFiniteMulSupport_def : HasFiniteMulSupport f ↔ f.mulSupport.Finite := Iff.rfl`. Do not tag it `@[simp]`, so that `fun_prop` goals and `HasFiniteMulSupport` hypotheses are not expanded unexpectedly. Then `simp [hasFiniteMulSupport_def]` or `rw [hasFiniteMulSupport_def]` rewrites to `f.mulSupport.Finite`. That form works with existing `mulSupport_*` simp lemmas and `Set.Finite` lemmas, and it doesn't unfold `mulSupport` itself. Replace the call sites that unfold by definition name, starting with `hasFiniteMulSupport_one`.
findings.benefit: There is one stable, discoverable bridge between the new predicate and the `Set.Finite`/`mulSupport` API. Downstream proofs no longer unfold the definition by name, so they would not break if it later changes, for example to a structure or a different underlying form. Users stop unfolding `mulSupport` down to `≠ 1` sets. The predicate also stays opaque to default simp, which keeps it usable with `fun_prop`.
